prediction_scored: miss. The NO2 DiD is +0.9% (-2.2 to +4.2), in the wrong direction and well inside the placebo distribution (one-sided p = 0.70); the refutation condition registered (estimate at or above 0) is met. The interval excludes the registered range below -2.2%, so the city data rule out an NO2 decline of the size seen in Stockholm, while allowing a small one. PM2.5: +1.7% (+0.0 to +3.3), also not a decline.
settle: The design compares model-based annual surfaces. NYCCAS is a land-use regression whose spatial covariates include traffic indicators held fixed across years and whose year-to-year change comes from street-level monitors adjusted to reference sites, so it may smooth a local change toward zero. Raw in-zone NYCCAS monitor values, a second post-year (2026), and hourly NO2 near the zone's main entry points would settle it.

notes: Group means, NO2 ppb: in zone {'2021': 21.84, '2022': 21.02, '2023': 22.07, '2024': 20.42, '2025': 20.57}; outside Manhattan {'2021': 16.04, '2022': 15.11, '2023': 15.87, '2024': 14.26, '2025': 14.63}. In-zone NO2 fell by 7.8 ppb (30.0 to 22.1) between 2014 and 2020, so the long-run decline is much larger than any 2025 change. The placebo-in-time (post = 2024) is +3.3% for NO2 and +12.8% for PM2.5; the PM2.5 series has a 2024 rise in the zone that the design cannot explain. Manhattan north of 60th St moved +5.9% in NO2 relative to outside Manhattan. This agrees with the DOHMH 2026 report, which used the same survey, and disagrees with Fraser et al. (2025) on PM2.5. Traffic speeds rose (mob-crz-traffic), so the policy changed traffic; the air-quality step of the chain is not visible in annual neighbourhood averages.
